Samsung Electronics has a new boss for its smartphone business. Co-CEO TM Roh is stepping down as head of the Mobile eXperience (MX) business and handing the role to Won-Joon Choi, who led development of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8 series.The change is part of Samsung ’s 2027 leadership reshuffle, announced on November 20. Roh isn’t going anywhere, though. He stays on as co-CEO and head of the Device eXperience (DX) division, and will now also focus on the company’s Robotics eXperience office. The idea, Samsung says, is to speed up new businesses like robotics.DX is the Samsung arm behind Galaxy phones, TVs and home appliances, while the Device Solutions (DS) division runs the chip business.Choi has been chief operating officer of MX since March 2025, so the phone business stays with someone who knows it from the inside. Under him, Samsung is expected to sharpen its focus on foldables, on-device AI and wearables.The bigger shake-up is on the semiconductor side, where three chip veterans have been promoted to president.Sang Joon Hwang, who led memory development across DRAM and high bandwidth memory (HBM), now heads the Memory business.Sangyeun Cho, who previously ran Samsung’s chip operations in the US, takes over System LSI, the unit that designs Exynos processors and camera sensors. Samsung is counting on his ties with global customers to win new clients.Jong Myeong Lee, a process engineer with about 28 years of experience across DRAM, NAND and foundry, becomes chief technology officer of DS and head of the semiconductor R&D centre.Vice Chairman Young Hyun Jun continues as co-CEO and head of DS. Now that Hwang is in charge of memory, Jun gives up his extra role as memory chief to concentrate on foundry and other future chip businesses.In all, six executives were named. Samsung says appointments at the vice president level and below, along with further organisational changes, will follow soon.
Article Summary: Co-CEO TM Roh is stepping down as head of the Mobile eXperience (MX) business. Won-Joon Choi, who led development of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8 series, will take over. Roh isn’t going anywhere, though, and will now focus on the company’s Robotics experience office.

Article Title: Meta gets a ‘China complaint’ from Taiwanese government; asked to check thousands of accounts that may be trying to...
Article Text:
Taiwan says China-linked accounts targeted its elections on Threads

Most of the flagged Threads accounts listed China as their location

AI-generated videos aimed at DPP politicians drew 2.35 million interactions'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Taiwan has handed Meta a list of nearly 2,700 social media accounts it believes are part of a Chinese information warfare campaign aimed at its local elections next week. The accounts are on Threads, Meta’s text-based app that is popular in Taiwan, and almost all were created in the past four months, Reuters reports, citing three government officials and internal reports.Meta says the accounts are gone. A company spokesperson told Reuters that many had already been disabled by its own systems, calling them “low-quality fake accounts” that had not posted about the elections. Most had no followers.The timing matters. Taiwan votes for mayors and county chiefs on November 28, and the results are seen as a test of support for President Lai Ching-te’s Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) ahead of the presidential election in early 2028. Beijing calls the DPP a “separatist” force and refuses to engage with it.One government report reviewed by Reuters looked at 2,400 of the Threads accounts. About 74% gave China as their location, roughly 25% gave none, and 1% listed Russia. The accounts fell into 27 clusters with similar Chinese names and different numerical IDs, which suggested they were created in bulk.Officials say Threads was targeted because of its popularity in Taiwan.No similar accounts turned up on Instagram.The accounts first posed as ordinary Taiwanese users, posting about everyday interests like fortune-telling. “Then one day, they start by criticising the government and attacking candidates, before saying they are disappointed with the ruling party and will therefore give up voting,” one official told Reuters.Taiwan also flagged about 260 accounts that it says pushed out more than 2,150 AI-generated videos as part of the same campaign. According to another internal report, those videos drew 2.35 million interactions, including comments and shares, and mostly targeted DPP politicians and policies.Some went after Puma Shen, the party’s candidate for Taipei mayor, accusing him of bullying when he was a student. Shen has denied the allegations.Three security officials told Reuters the aim was less about backing candidates and more about turning people against each other and putting them off voting. All spoke on condition of anonymity.A National Security Council official said Taipei would keep working with allies and platforms to keep foreign forces from swaying its elections. China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment. Beijing has long denied interfering in Taiwan’s elections.
Article Summary: Taiwan says China-linked accounts targeted its elections on Threads. Most of the flagged Threads accounts listed China as their location.AI-generated videos aimed at DPP politicians drew 2.35 million interactions. Taipei will keep working with allies and platforms to keep foreign forces from swaying its elections.

Dell Technologies on Friday launched the XPS 16 Creator Edition in India, the first XPS laptop to run on NVIDIA’s RTX Spark superchip. The Windows laptop is aimed at video editors, 3D artists and AI developers who want to run large AI models on the machine itself instead of relying on the cloud. It starts at Rs 4,49,990 including taxes and is on sale from today at Dellstore.com, with a wider retail rollout planned for mid-December. Dell says the laptop packs a high-end graphics processor, a CPU and up to 128GB of shared memory into a chassis just 17.8mm thin, and pairs them with a colour-accurate OLED display and a full set of ports for professional work.The RTX Spark superchip combines up to a 6,144-core NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU, up to a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU and up to 128GB of unified memory, according to Dell. Because the CPU and GPU share one large memory pool, Dell says creators can work with massive 3D scenes, multi-layer 8K timelines and large AI models that would exceed the limits of a traditional laptop with a separate graphics card. The chip also includes real-time ray tracing, DLSS and native 4:2:2 hardware encode and decode. The body is CNC-machined aluminium.The laptop has a 3.2K tandem OLED display that Dell says is built for colour-critical work.It supports VESA DisplayHDR True Black 600 with peak brightness up to 1,000 nits, covers 100% of the DCI-P3 colour gamut, and is factory calibrated to Delta E below 2 with Pantone Validation. The refresh rate varies from 20Hz to 120Hz, dropping to 20Hz on static content to save battery.For connectivity, it has a full-size SDXC v7.1 card reader, three USB4 Type-C ports with DisplayPort 2.1 and Power Delivery that can charge the laptop from any port, an HDMI 2.1b port that supports up to three external displays, and a universal audio jack.The laptop includes the full NVIDIA CUDA software stack. Dell says developers can prototype, fine-tune and run inference on the latest AI models locally on up to 128GB of memory, using the same architecture found in production AI environments. Dell says developer tools including GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, ComfyUI and Cursor run on RTX Spark, and that Windows provides identity, containment, manageability and user controls for running AI models and agents locally.RTX Spark Windows PCs run native applications and also run x86 applications through Prism emulation. Dell says Blender, DaVinci Resolve, Adobe Photoshop and Adobe Premiere run natively, while applications such as MATLAB are supported through Prism. For gaming, the platform supports the Easy Anti-Cheat and BattlEye anti-cheat systems and the Xbox PC app.Anurag Arora, senior director and general manager of Consumer Sales in India at Dell Technologies, said India’s professional creators are editing multi-layer 8K timelines and rendering complex 3D scenes, and increasingly layering AI-driven workflows on top. He said the XPS 16 Creator Edition is “purpose-built” for that kind of work and sets a new benchmark for a premium creative laptop.The XPS 16 Creator Edition starts at Rs 4,49,990 including taxes. Buyers can get up to Rs 15,000 cashback through Axis Bank and ICICI Bank, and zero down payment finance options are available. It is on sale now at Dellstore.com and will reach Dell Exclusive Stores, large-format retail and e-tail by mid-December.

Article Title: Verizon CEO said SpaceX will need hundreds of billions to just compete with his company; Elon Musk responds to him from China; says: We will build ...
Article Text:
“No secret sauce”

Elon Musk points to micro cell towers

How the plan came together

Analysts see limited near-term risk

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Verizon’s response: be ready

Verizon CEO Dan Schulman has taken aim at Elon Musk ’s plan to turn Starlink into a major US mobile carrier, saying that if Musk succeeds, he will have spent four to six years and roughly $300 billion building what amounts to a replica of Verizon’s network. In an interview with Fortune, Schulman argued that SpaceX would gain no special cost advantage and would simply become the sixth player in a market already crowded with three mobile operators and two big cable companies. His comments come weeks after SpaceX’s announcement wiped about $50 billion off the market value of the three major US carriers, and as Musk is now discussing hardware that could make Starlink look even more like a traditional operator.Schulman made the remarks on Fortune’s Titans and Disruptors of Industry podcast, speaking with Editor in Chief Alyson Shontell. He said Musk could end up with a network “pretty much exactly like our network today,” with no structural cost advantage to show for the investment. In his view, SpaceX would enter the market years from now as just another entrant.Musk gave more detail on Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit.He said SpaceX is looking at producing “micro cell towers” for Starlink Mobile as early as next year. Schulman has said this kind of ground equipment is what turns SpaceX into just another carrier.SpaceX said in October that Starlink would become a major US mobile carrier. Telecom stocks fell sharply, and Fortune reported that the three big US carriers lost about $50 billion in combined market value. Verizon dropped 8.7%, its worst single day since 2002.The groundwork was laid in September 2025, when SpaceX bought wireless spectrum from EchoStar in a $17 billion deal, which the FCC approved in May. Starlink Mobile would differ from other carriers by connecting phones directly to satellites, with no dish or router. The October announcement also said the FCC had approved 15,000 new satellite launches for the service and that SpaceX had bought additional low-band spectrum licences from Grain Management. Starlink has 12 million paying subscribers and is the only profitable part of SpaceX’s business as of its latest earnings, Fortune said.In a note to investors last month, JPMorgan analysts said that without a deal with an existing carrier, SpaceX would have to build its own ground network, which would take even more capital than it is already spending on spectrum. They said they see limited near-term risk to US wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital involved.Schulman further added that the market is already competitive and expects it to look “radically different” in three or four years as 6G arrives and AI is built into networks. He said that Verizon will have to continue moving whether SpaceX becomes a major player or not. He feels that is the only sensible way to assume SpaceX will deliver on what it says, because the real danger is complacency. He also mentioned that he has not spoken to Elin Musk recently and he is also not sure of his strategy. Musk could, for example, invest further in data centers in space or pursue other high-return options. Schulman said his message to Verizon staff is to prepare for every scenario and “shape the market, not react.”
Article Summary: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman has taken aim at Elon Musk’s plan to turn Starlink into a major US mobile carrier. He said Musk could end up with a network “pretty much exactly like our network today,” with no structural cost advantage to show for the investment. In his view, SpaceX would enter the market years from now as just another entrant.

Article Title: US 'China ban' expands: After Nvidia, two of world’s biggest chipmakers pause shipments
Article Text:
AI chip (Representative image)

Closing loopholes on AI data center chips

Smartphone makers caught in the crossfire

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and Samsung Electronics have reportedly paused shipments of certain chips to clients in China following fresh US export rules aimed at slowing Beijing’s artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions. In recent days, both chipmaking giants notified Chinese customers that deliveries of specific processors are on hold while they apply for export licenses from the US Commerce Department, The Financial Times reported citing multiple people briefed on the matter. The halt adds fresh pressure on Chinese tech firms, which are already dealing with component shortages caused by a surge in memory chip prices and tight production capacity at local suppliers like Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).The move stems from a new regulation issued this week by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US Commerce Department agency overseeing sensitive technologies. Under the rule, any chipmaker using American technology to produce advanced chips must now apply for a license before selling products that end up with customers in China. These include the datacenter operators in counties including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Commerce Department said in a statement.Previously, even as Washington restricted exports of top-tier processors, some Chinese chip designers worked around the rules by routing orders for high-performance AI data center chips through independent packaging and testing firms. Those third-party companies would verify that the designs fell outside US restrictions, bypassing the need for direct government approval. The new BIS rule shuts down that pathway entirely.Among Samsung’s Chinese clients affected by the tightening supply are Baidu’s AI data center unit, Kunlun, and TikTok parent company ByteDance – both of which have been looking to diversify their chip sources due to growing shortages of Nvidia processors in China.The restrictions aren’t just hitting AI companies. TSMC and Samsung have also alerted consumer electronics customers that shipments are suspended, according to two people familiar with the situation.The updated BIS rule removes earlier exemptions that allowed companies to prove chips were meant for non-AI uses, such as smartphones, rather than restricted AI computing. According to a lawyer briefed on the matter, dropping that exemption means TSMC and Samsung must now obtain U.S. licenses even for consumer chips built using advanced manufacturing processes.TSMC produces smartphone processors for major Chinese brands including Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo. The Financial Times reported that while an industry insider noted that the US Commerce Department will likely grant licenses for consumer smartphone chips eventually, the approval process is expected to trigger major manufacturing delays.
Article Summary: TSMC and Samsung have reportedly paused shipments of certain chips to clients in China following fresh US export rules. The move stems from a new regulation issued this week by the US Commerce Department agency overseeing sensitive technologies. Under the rule, any chipmaker using American technology to produce advanced chips must now apply for a license.
